stem: A hospital wants to sample patient discharges and is sure that the three wards discharge patients differently. It takes a random sample from each ward separately. Which sampling method is this?
options: Simple random sampling
Convenience sampling
Systematic sampling
Stratified sampling
explanation: Dividing the population into groups (strata) expected to differ and sampling randomly within each is stratified sampling. It guarantees every ward is represented and lets the wards be compared (Day 6).
distractor_notes: Simple random sampling would draw from all discharges together, and could under-represent a small ward.
Convenience sampling takes whatever is easiest, and is not a valid method.
Systematic sampling takes every k-th unit.

stem: To estimate the error rate in last month's 3,000 invoices, a clerk checks the 100 invoices that customers have already queried. What is wrong with this sample?
options: It is biased: queried invoices are more likely to contain errors, so the estimate will be too high
It is too small: a proportion needs at least 500 observations
It is stratified: only one stratum (queried invoices) was sampled, which is acceptable
It is systematic: every 30th invoice was checked, so periodic errors are missed
explanation: The invoices were selected because something was already wrong with them, so they do not represent the 3 000. That is sampling bias from convenience sampling. Taking more queried invoices would not help; the selection method must change to random or stratified (Day 6).
distractor_notes: Size is not the main problem; even a large biased sample is wrong.
One self-selected group is not a stratum; the sample is convenience-based and biased.
Nothing was taken at a fixed interval.

stem: A bottling line has 12 filling heads that fill in rotation. A technician samples every 12th bottle for weight. What is the risk with this plan?
options: The sample will contain too many bottles from the fastest head
Every sampled bottle comes from the same filling head, so the other 11 heads are never checked
The sample will be too small to estimate the mean weight
The sample will over-represent the last bottles of each shift
explanation: Systematic sampling fails when the process has a cycle that matches the sampling interval (periodicity). Every 12th bottle here is always from one head. Using an interval that does not divide the cycle, or random sampling, avoids it (Day 6).
distractor_notes: Every 12th bottle is always the same head, not the fastest one.
Sample size is unrelated to the interval problem.
The interval matches the head cycle, not the shift.

stem: A sample was taken by convenience and is known to be unrepresentative. Which of the following would fix the problem?
options: Selecting the units by a proper random or stratified method instead
Taking ten times as many units the same way
Reporting the median instead of the mean
Calculating the sample standard deviation with n − 1
explanation: Sampling bias is a property of the selection method. A bigger biased sample is still biased; only changing how units are chosen removes it. Statistical corrections operate on the numbers, not on who was chosen (Day 6).
distractor_notes: Size does not cure bias.
The median is robust to outliers, not to a biased sample.
The n − 1 divisor corrects the standard deviation estimate, not the selection.

stem: What defines a simple random sample?
options: Every k-th unit is selected after a random start
Units are chosen by an experienced inspector as typical of the process
Units are drawn from each subgroup in proportion to its size
Every unit has an equal chance of selection, made by a chance mechanism
explanation: Simple random sampling gives every unit an equal chance and uses random numbers or an equivalent chance device, not human choice. It needs a list of the population. Inspector choice is judgement sampling; every k-th is systematic; nearest is convenience (Day 6).
distractor_notes: That is systematic sampling.
That is judgement sampling, which reproduces the inspector's assumptions.
That is stratified sampling.

stem: A sample of 36 invoices has a standard deviation of 6.0 minutes. What is the standard error of the mean?
options: 1.00 minute
0.33 minutes
0.17 minutes
6.00 minutes
explanation: Standard error = s ÷ √n = 6.0 ÷ √36 = 6.0 ÷ 6 = 1.00 minute. Sample means scatter far less than individual invoices (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 0.33 divides by 18, a wrong square root.
0.17 divides by n (36) instead of √n.
6.00 is the standard deviation of individual values, not of the mean.

stem: What does the central limit theorem state?
options: Sample means are approximately normal with standard deviation σ ÷ √n, whatever the population's shape
Any sample of 30 or more values is itself normally distributed
The population mean equals the sample mean once n exceeds 30
Sample means have the same spread as individual values when n is large
explanation: The theorem is about the sampling distribution of the mean: its centre is μ, its spread is the standard error σ ÷ √n, and its shape approaches normal as n grows, regardless of the population's shape. It is why normal-based tools work on averages of non-normal data (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Individual values keep the population's shape; only their means become normal.
The sample mean estimates μ but does not equal it.
Means have a smaller spread, σ ÷ √n, than individual values.

stem: Repair times are strongly right-skewed. A Green Belt takes many samples of 40 repairs and plots the sample means. What shape will the plot of means have?
options: Bimodal, with short and long repairs separated
Right-skewed, like the individual repair times
Approximately normal, as the central limit theorem predicts for means
Left-skewed, as the averaging reverses the tail
explanation: With n = 40 the means of skewed data are close to normally distributed, centred on the population mean with spread σ ÷ √40. The individual repair times stay skewed; it is their averages that become normal (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Two peaks would need two mixed populations, not skew.
Skew in the individual values is largely averaged out in means of 40.
Averaging reduces skew; it does not reverse it.

stem: A sample of 36 invoices has a mean processing time of 42.0 minutes and a standard deviation of 6.0 minutes. Using a t critical value of 2.03, what is the upper limit of the 95% confidence interval for the mean?
options: 54.18 minutes
48.00 minutes
44.03 minutes
43.00 minutes
explanation: Standard error = 6 ÷ √36 = 1.0. Margin of error = 2.03 × 1.0 = 2.03. Upper limit = 42.0 + 2.03 = 44.03 minutes; the full interval is 39.97 to 44.03 (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 54.18 uses the standard deviation (6) instead of the standard error (1).
48.00 adds the standard deviation itself.
43.00 adds one standard error without the critical value.

stem: What is statistical inference?
options: Drawing conclusions about a population from a sample, with stated uncertainty
Displaying a data set on a histogram or box plot
Summarising a data set with its mean and standard deviation
Choosing the sampling method and sample size for a study
explanation: Descriptive statistics summarise the sample; inference goes further and says what the sample implies about the population, through confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, with the uncertainty stated (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Plotting is graphical analysis.
That is descriptive statistics.
Sampling design comes before inference.

stem: A 95% confidence interval for the mean fill weight is 249.2 g to 251.6 g. The target is 250 g. What can be concluded?
options: The process mean differs significantly from 250 g at α = 0.05
95% of individual bottles weigh between 249.2 g and 251.6 g
A mean of 250 g is consistent with the data; a two-tailed test at α = 0.05 would not reject
The process mean is exactly 250 g, since 250 lies inside the interval
explanation: The interval contains 250, so the data do not contradict a mean of 250. A confidence interval that includes the hypothesised value corresponds to a two-tailed test that fails to reject at the matching alpha. The interval is about the mean, not about individual bottles (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Significance would need the interval to exclude 250.
The interval describes where the population mean lies, not the spread of individual bottles.
The interval gives a range, not an exact value.

stem: The standard error of the mean for a sample of 36 (standard deviation 6.0) is 1.00. If the sample size is increased to 144, what is the new standard error?
explanation: Standard error = 6 ÷ √144 = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.50. Quadrupling the sample halves the standard error, because it depends on the square root of n (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 1.00 is the original standard error.
0.25 assumes the error falls in proportion to n; it falls with √n.
0.04 divides by n.

subtopic: General Concepts & Goals of Hypothesis Testing
stem: In a hypothesis test comparing two shifts' mean output, what does the null hypothesis state?
options: The difference is practically significant
The two shifts have the same mean output
Shift A has higher mean output than shift B
The two shifts have different mean output
explanation: The null hypothesis is always the statement of no effect or no difference: the means are equal. The alternative states the difference the test is trying to demonstrate (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Practical significance is judged separately from the test.
A directional claim is a one-tailed alternative.
A difference is the alternative hypothesis.

subtopic: General Concepts & Goals of Hypothesis Testing
stem: A test gives p = 0.31 with alpha = 0.05. Which is the correct statement of the conclusion?
options: Declare the test inconclusive, since p is between 0.05 and 0.50
Accept the null hypothesis, since the data show the means are equal
Fail to reject the null hypothesis, since the data do not show a difference
Reject the null hypothesis, since p is above alpha
explanation: p is above alpha, so H₀ is not rejected. The wording matters: the data have failed to show a difference, which is not proof that there is none, so H₀ is never "accepted" (Day 14).
distractor_notes: A clear non-significant result is a valid conclusion, not an error.
"Accept" claims proof of no difference, which a non-significant result cannot give.
Rejection needs p at or below alpha, not above it.

subtopic: General Concepts & Goals of Hypothesis Testing
stem: A hypothesis test returns p = 0.03. Alpha was set at 0.05. What is the decision?
options: Fail to reject the null hypothesis: the result is not significant
Raise alpha to 0.10 and repeat the test
Accept the alternative hypothesis with 97% certainty
Reject the null hypothesis: the result is significant at the 5% level
explanation: p ≤ α, so the null hypothesis is rejected and the result is significant at the 5% level. The p-value is not the probability that the alternative is true, and alpha is fixed before the test (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 0.03 is below 0.05, so H₀ is rejected.
Alpha is chosen before the data are seen and is not adjusted afterwards.
A p-value is not the probability that either hypothesis is true.

subtopic: General Concepts & Goals of Hypothesis Testing
stem: What is a p-value?
options: The proportion of the sample that falls outside the specification limits
The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true, given the data
The probability that the null hypothesis is true, given the data
The probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed, if the null hypothesis were true
explanation: The p-value measures how surprising the data would be under H₀. A small p-value means the data are unlikely if H₀ holds, so H₀ is rejected. It is not the probability of either hypothesis (Day 14).
distractor_notes: That is a defect proportion, unrelated to p-values.
Same error for the alternative.
The p-value is conditional on H₀ being true; it is not its probability.

stem: Comparing 5,000 invoices from each of two systems, the mean processing times are 40.2 and 40.0 minutes, p = 0.001. What should the Green Belt conclude?
options: The difference is statistically significant and practically important
The difference is practically important but not statistically significant
The difference is statistically significant but practically unimportant
The difference is neither statistically significant nor practically important
explanation: Very large samples detect tiny differences: p = 0.001 says the 0.2-minute gap is unlikely to be chance, not that it matters. Practical significance is judged from the effect size against the business case (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 0.2 minutes on a 40-minute process is not practically significant.
p = 0.001 is far below 0.05, so it is statistically significant.
It is statistically significant; it is the practical importance that is lacking.

stem: What is the difference between statistical significance and practical significance?
options: Statistical significance means the effect is large; practical significance means it is real
They are the same thing expressed in different units
Statistical significance means the effect is unlikely to be chance; practical significance means the effect is large enough to matter
Practical significance is measured by the p-value
explanation: A p-value addresses whether an effect could be chance. Whether the effect is worth acting on depends on its size and the business case, which the p-value does not measure. Both must be reported (Day 14).
distractor_notes: This reverses the two.
They answer different questions.
The p-value measures statistical significance only.

stem: A pilot compared 8 orders processed by a new method with 8 by the old. The new method averaged 12 minutes faster, but the test gave p = 0.14. The Champion says "so the new method makes no difference". What is the best response?
options: Disagree: with n = 8 the test has little power, so a real 12-minute gain could easily be missed
Agree, provided the data in both groups were normally distributed
Agree: a p-value above 0.05 shows the methods do not differ
Disagree: a 12-minute difference is always significant whatever the p-value
explanation: A non-significant result with a tiny sample usually means the test lacked power to detect the effect, not that the effect is absent. The 12-minute difference is practically important, so the right step is a larger sample (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Normality does not rescue the sample size problem.
Non-significance is not proof of no effect.
Significance depends on the p-value; the argument here is about power, not about the size alone.

stem: What is a Type I error?
options: Drawing a sample that is too small to detect the effect
Failing to reject a null hypothesis that is false
Rejecting a null hypothesis that is true
Using a one-tailed test where a two-tailed test was needed
explanation: A Type I error is a false alarm, and its probability is alpha. A Type II error is the reverse: missing an effect that is real, with probability beta (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Small samples raise beta (Type II risk), not Type I.
That is a Type II error.
That is a design mistake, not a Type I error.

stem: Alpha is set at 0.05. What does this value represent?
options: The probability computed from the sample data
The probability of failing to detect a real effect
The probability of rejecting a null hypothesis that is true
The probability that the test detects a real effect
explanation: Alpha is the significance level and equals the probability of a Type I error, a false alarm. Beta is the Type II risk and power is 1 − beta. The p-value is calculated from the data and compared with alpha (Day 14).
distractor_notes: The p-value comes from the data; alpha is chosen in advance.
The Type II error probability is beta.
Power is 1 − beta.

stem: A test has beta = 0.20. What is its power, and what does power mean?
options: 0.05: the probability of a Type I error
0.95: the confidence level
0.20: the probability of a false alarm
0.80: the probability of detecting an effect that really exists
explanation: Power = 1 − beta = 0.80: an 80% chance of rejecting H₀ when it is false. Power rises with larger samples, larger effects and higher alpha (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 0.05 would be alpha.
Confidence level is 1 − alpha, a different quantity.
0.20 is beta, the probability of missing a real effect.

stem: A team tested a new adhesive, concluded at p = 0.04 that it was stronger, and switched production to it. Six months later a larger study shows the two adhesives are equally strong. Which error did the team most likely make?
options: A Type I error: they rejected a true null hypothesis
A sampling bias: their sample was unrepresentative
A Type II error: they missed a real difference
A power error: their sample was too small to detect anything
explanation: The original test found an effect that later evidence shows was not real: a false alarm, which is a Type I error. With alpha = 0.05, one test in twenty on a true null hypothesis will do this by chance (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Nothing suggests the sample was unrepresentative; the result was chance at the 4% level.
A Type II error would be missing a real difference.
Low power causes missed effects, not false alarms.

stem: A team wants to know whether a new supplier's parts are stronger than the current supplier's parts. Which alternative hypothesis and test type are appropriate?
options: H₁: new mean > current mean; one-tailed
H₁: new mean = current mean; one-tailed
H₁: new mean < current mean; two-tailed
H₁: the means differ; two-tailed
explanation: The question has a direction (stronger), so the alternative is one-sided and the test is one-tailed, with all of alpha in the upper tail. The direction must be fixed before the data are examined (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Equality is the null hypothesis, not the alternative.
The direction is the wrong way, and a directional H₁ is one-tailed.
"Differ" would be two-tailed and is a weaker question than the one asked.

stem: A two-tailed test gives p = 0.053. If the same data are analysed with a one-tailed test in the direction of the observed difference, what is the p-value?
explanation: For the same data, the one-tailed p-value is half the two-tailed value: 0.053 ÷ 2 = 0.0265. That is why the tail must be chosen before seeing the data: switching afterwards turns a non-significant result into a significant one (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 0.053 is the two-tailed value unchanged.
0.106 doubles instead of halving.
0.0135 quarters it.

stem: Ten machines are measured for output before and after a maintenance change. Which type of test compares the before and after results?
options: A one-way ANOVA with before and after as two levels
A one-sample test of the after values against the before mean
A two-sample test treating before and after as independent groups
A paired test on the before-minus-after difference for each machine
explanation: The before and after readings come from the same machines, so the natural analysis is on the differences within each machine: a paired test. Treating them as two independent samples wastes the pairing and loses power (Day 14).
distractor_notes: ANOVA on two dependent groups has the same flaw as the two-sample test.
The before mean is not a fixed target; it is itself a sample.
The two sets are not independent; the same machines appear in both.

stem: A filling line is required to average 250 g. A sample of 30 bottles is weighed to check this. Which type of test is this?
options: A paired test comparing each bottle before and after filling
A one-sample test comparing the sample mean with the target of 250 g
A test of proportions on the share of bottles under 250 g
A two-sample test comparing this sample with last month's sample
explanation: One sample is compared with a fixed value, so it is a one-sample test (a one-sample t-test on Day 16). Two-sample and paired tests compare two sets of data; proportions apply to pass/fail data (Day 14).
distractor_notes: Nothing is measured twice on the same units.
Weight is continuous, not a proportion.
There is only one sample; the other side is a fixed target.

stem: For a one-tailed test at alpha = 0.05, what is the critical Z value?
explanation: With all 5% in one tail, the critical Z has 0.95 below it: 1.645. The two-tailed 5% value is 1.96 (2.5% in each tail); 2.576 is two-tailed 1%; 1.282 is one-tailed 10% (Day 14).
distractor_notes: 1.960 is the two-tailed 5% value.
2.576 is the two-tailed 1% value.
1.282 is the one-tailed 10% value.

stem: Ten pumps are tested for flow rate, then fitted with a new seal, then tested again. Which test compares the flow rates before and after?
options: 2-sample t-test with before and after as independent groups
One-way ANOVA with pump as the factor
Paired t-test on each pump's before-minus-after difference
1-sample t-test against the before mean
explanation: The same ten pumps are measured twice, so the natural analysis is on each pump's difference: a paired t-test. Treating the two columns as independent samples throws away the pairing and loses power (Day 16).
distractor_notes: The two sets are not independent; the same pumps appear in both.
ANOVA compares three or more independent groups.
The before mean is itself a sample, not a fixed target.

stem: A sample of 36 invoices has a mean processing time of 42.0 minutes and a standard deviation of 6.0 minutes. Test whether the mean is 40 minutes. What is the t statistic?
explanation: t = (x̄ − μ₀) ÷ (s ÷ √n) = (42 − 40) ÷ (6 ÷ 6) = 2 ÷ 1 = 2.00, with 35 degrees of freedom (Day 16).
distractor_notes: 0.06 divides by n.
0.33 divides by s instead of the standard error s ÷ √n.
12.00 multiplies by √n instead of dividing s by it.

stem: For the 1-sample t-test with t = 2.00 on 35 degrees of freedom (two-tailed), what is the p-value, and is the result significant at alpha = 0.05?
options: 0.1066; not significant
0.0267; significant
0.0500; significant
0.0533; not significant
explanation: The two-tailed p-value for t = 2.00 with 35 df is 0.053, slightly above 0.05, so H₀ is not rejected. The one-tailed value would be 0.027 (Day 16).
distractor_notes: 0.1066 doubles the two-tailed value.
0.0267 is the one-tailed p-value; the test is two-tailed.
The p-value is not exactly 0.05, and at 0.053 it does not reach significance.

stem: Software output for a 2-sample t-test shows DF = 32 although the samples have 20 and 18 observations. What does this indicate?
options: A paired test was used on 32 matched pairs
The pooled test was used, and 32 is n₁ + n₂ − 2 with a typing error
Welch's test was used, which lowers the degrees of freedom below n₁ + n₂ − 2
Four observations were removed as outliers before the test was run
explanation: The pooled test would report 36 degrees of freedom. Welch's version, which does not assume equal variances, calculates a smaller df from the two variances and sample sizes; a reduced or non-integer DF is the signature of Welch (Day 16).
distractor_notes: A paired test needs equal sample sizes and would report pairs − 1.
20 + 18 − 2 is 36, and software does not mistype degrees of freedom.
Software does not silently discard observations.

stem: Day shift: n = 20, mean 38.2, standard deviation 5.1. Night shift: n = 18, mean 42.9, standard deviation 6.4. What is the Welch 2-sample t statistic (day minus night)?
distractor_notes: −0.82 divides the difference by the sum of the standard deviations.
−1.24 uses a doubled standard error.
−4.70 is the raw difference in means, not divided by its standard error.

stem: A pooled 2-sample t-test compares samples of 20 and 18. What are the degrees of freedom?
explanation: For the pooled test, df = n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 20 + 18 − 2 = 36 (Day 16).
distractor_notes: 37 subtracts only 1.
38 is the total sample size.
17 is the smaller sample minus 1, a conservative approximation sometimes used for Welch, not the pooled df.

stem:
Output from a 2-sample t-test comparing cycle times (minutes) reads:

```
Estimate for difference:  -4.70
95% CI for difference:  (-8.55, -0.85)
T-Test of difference = 0 (vs not =): T-Value = -2.49  P-Value = 0.018  DF = 32
```

What is the conclusion at alpha = 0.05?
options: Fail to reject H₀; the negative t value shows no effect
Fail to reject H₀; the interval shows the difference could be zero
Reject H₀; the first group's mean is higher by about 4.7 minutes
Reject H₀; the second group's mean is higher by about 4.7 minutes
explanation: p = 0.018 is below 0.05, so the means differ. The estimate is group 1 minus group 2 = −4.7, so group 2 is higher. The interval (−8.55, −0.85) excludes zero, consistent with rejecting (Day 16).
distractor_notes: A negative t only shows the direction of the difference; p = 0.018 rejects.
The interval excludes zero and p < 0.05.
A negative difference (group 1 minus group 2) means group 1 is lower.

stem: Ten clerks were timed before and after a change. The before-minus-after differences (seconds) are 3.1, −0.4, 2.2, 1.8, 0.6, 2.9, 1.1, −0.2, 2.4, 1.5 (mean 1.50, standard deviation 1.22). What is the paired t statistic?
distractor_notes: 12.30 multiplies by n instead of √n.
0.39 divides the standard error by the mean.
1.23 divides by s_d without √n.

stem: A sample of 25 parts has variance 0.36. The historical variance is 0.25. What is the chi-square statistic for the 1-sample variance test?
explanation: χ² = (n − 1) × s² ÷ σ₀² = 24 × 0.36 ÷ 0.25 = 24 × 1.44 = 34.56 with 24 degrees of freedom (Day 16).
distractor_notes: 1.44 is the variance ratio without the degrees of freedom.
17.36 uses standard deviations (0.6 ÷ 0.5) instead of variances.
36.00 uses n instead of n − 1.

stem: Which distribution and degrees of freedom does the 1-sample variance test use?
options: The chi-square distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom
The F distribution with n₁ − 1 and n₂ − 1 degrees of freedom
The normal distribution
The t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom
explanation: The statistic (n − 1)s² ÷ σ₀² follows a chi-square distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom when the data are normal. The F distribution is for comparing two variances; t is for means (Day 16).
distractor_notes: F with two df values is the two-variance test.
The normal distribution is not used for a variance test.
t is for means, not variances.

stem: A team hopes a new fixture has reduced the variance of a dimension from the historical 0.25. A sample of 25 parts gives s² = 0.16. The one-sided test (H₁: σ² < 0.25) gives χ² = 15.36 with 24 df, p = 0.09. What should the team conclude?
options: The test cannot be applied because the sample variance is below the historical value
The variance has been reduced, since 0.16 is well below 0.25
The variance has increased, since the chi-square value is above 12.4
The reduction is not statistically established at alpha = 0.05; a larger sample is needed
explanation: p = 0.09 > 0.05: fail to reject H₀. The sample variance is lower, but with 25 parts the reduction is not statistically established. Variance tests need larger samples than mean tests to detect a change (Day 16).
distractor_notes: The one-sided test is exactly for this case.
A lower sample variance is not proof; the p-value says it could be chance.
15.36 is in the lower part of the distribution; nothing suggests an increase.

stem: Why is the t distribution used instead of the normal distribution for a 1-sample test of a mean?
options: Because the t distribution is narrower and so gives smaller p-values
Because the t distribution has no degrees of freedom to look up
Because sample means are never normally distributed
Because the population standard deviation is estimated from the sample, which adds uncertainty
explanation: When σ is estimated by s, the test statistic varies more than a Z would, especially with small samples. The t distribution is wider to allow for that, converging on the normal as degrees of freedom grow (Day 16).
distractor_notes: t is wider than the normal, giving larger p-values, not smaller.
The t distribution depends on degrees of freedom.
Sample means are approximately normal by the central limit theorem.

stem: Which of the following is an assumption of the 2-sample t-test?
options: The two samples are drawn from the same population
The observations are independent and each group is roughly normal or reasonably large
The two samples have exactly the same number of observations
The two population means are equal before the test is run
explanation: Independence within and between samples and approximate normality (or a sample large enough for the central limit theorem) are the assumptions. Equal means is the null hypothesis, not an assumption; equal sizes are not required (Day 16).
distractor_notes: The samples come from two populations that may differ; that is the point of the test.
Unequal sample sizes are fine.
Equal means is H₀, what the test examines, not an assumption.

stem: A team wants to compare the mean cycle times of four suppliers. Why is one-way ANOVA preferred to running a 2-sample t-test on each pair?
options: ANOVA does not require the residuals to be normal
ANOVA needs smaller samples than six t-tests would
t-tests cannot be used when the samples are of different sizes
Six separate t-tests inflate the overall Type I risk; ANOVA uses one alpha for all means
explanation: Four groups give six pairs, and six tests at 5% each carry about a 26% chance of at least one false alarm. ANOVA tests the single hypothesis that all means are equal with one alpha, then post-hoc comparisons handle the pairs (Day 17).
distractor_notes: ANOVA assumes roughly normal residuals.
Sample size requirements are similar.
t-tests work with unequal sizes.

stem: A one-way ANOVA compares 3 clerks with 6 observations each (18 in total). What are the degrees of freedom for the error (within-group) row?
explanation: df within = N − k = 18 − 3 = 15. The factor row has k − 1 = 2 and the total has N − 1 = 17; 2 + 15 = 17 (Day 17).
distractor_notes: 17 is the total degrees of freedom.
2 is the factor (between) degrees of freedom.
5 is one group's observations minus 1, not the pooled error df.

stem: In an ANOVA table the factor row has SS = 360 and DF = 2. What is the factor mean square?
explanation: Mean square = sum of squares ÷ degrees of freedom = 360 ÷ 2 = 180 (Day 17).
distractor_notes: 720 multiplies instead of dividing.
360 is the sum of squares itself.
120 divides by 3, the number of groups, instead of k − 1.

stem: An ANOVA has SS between = 360 with 2 df and SS within = 180 with 15 df. What is the F statistic?
distractor_notes: 30.0 divides MS between by the within df instead of MS within.
0.067 inverts the ratio.
2.0 divides the sums of squares (360 ÷ 180) without the degrees of freedom.

stem: An ANOVA has SS between = 360 and SS total = 540. What proportion of the variation in Y is explained by the factor (R-squared)?
explanation: R² = SS between ÷ SS total = 360 ÷ 540 = 0.667: two-thirds of the variation is between groups (Day 17).
distractor_notes: 0.333 is SS within ÷ SS total, the unexplained share.
2.000 divides SS between by SS within.
0.500 would need equal between and within sums of squares.

stem: What is the alternative hypothesis in a one-way ANOVA comparing four suppliers?
options: All four supplier means are different from each other
The four variances are equal
Supplier A has the highest mean
At least one supplier mean differs from the others
explanation: ANOVA's H₁ is that the means are not all equal: at least one differs. It does not say which, or that all differ; Tukey's comparisons answer that (Day 17).
distractor_notes: "All different" is stronger than H₁; one differing is enough.
Equal variances is an assumption, not the hypothesis.
ANOVA is not directional about a specific group.

stem:
ANOVA output for entry time by clerk reads:

```
Source   DF     SS     MS      F      P
Clerk     2  360.0  180.0  15.00  0.000
Error    15  180.0   12.0
Total    17  540.0

Tukey grouping: Ben A;  Ana B;  Chen B
```

What is the correct conclusion?
options: The clerks differ; Ben differs from Ana and Chen, who do not differ from each other
Ana differs from Chen, but Ben does not differ from either
The clerks do not differ, because the p-value is printed as 0.000
All three clerks differ significantly from each other
explanation: p < 0.001 rejects equal means. In the Tukey grouping, groups sharing a letter are not significantly different: Ana and Chen share B, Ben alone has A, so Ben is the one that differs (Day 17).
distractor_notes: The letters show the opposite.
0.000 means p < 0.0005: highly significant, so the clerks do differ.
Ana and Chen share a grouping letter, so they do not differ.

stem: After a significant one-way ANOVA, what is the purpose of Tukey's test?
options: To check that the residuals are normally distributed
To test whether the group variances are equal
To compare every pair of means while holding the overall Type I risk at alpha
To calculate the F statistic from the mean squares
explanation: A significant F says at least one mean differs. Tukey's honest significant difference gives confidence intervals for all pairwise differences with the overall alpha protected, and grouping letters show which groups differ (Day 17).
distractor_notes: Residual normality is checked with a probability plot.
Variance equality is checked with Levene's or Bartlett's test.
F comes from the ANOVA table.

stem: An ANOVA gives F = 15.0 with 2 and 15 degrees of freedom. What is the critical F at alpha = 0.05, and what is the decision?
options: 4.54; reject H₀
6.36; reject H₀ only at alpha = 0.01
3.68; reject H₀ because 15.0 exceeds it
19.4; fail to reject because 15.0 is below it
explanation: The F table at (2, 15) df and α = 0.05 gives 3.68. F = 15.0 is far beyond it, so H₀ (equal means) is rejected; the p-value is about 0.0003 (Day 17).
distractor_notes: 4.54 is the critical F at (2, 15) for alpha = 0.025, or a misread row.
6.36 is the critical F at alpha = 0.01; the question asks for alpha = 0.05, and F = 15.0 exceeds both anyway.
19.4 is the critical F with the degrees of freedom reversed (15, 2).

stem: Which of the following is an assumption of one-way ANOVA, and what is the non-parametric alternative if the data are clearly non-normal with small samples?
options: Equal sample sizes; the paired t-test is the alternative
Equal group means; the chi-square test is the alternative
Independent factor levels; regression is the alternative
Similar variances and roughly normal residuals; Kruskal-Wallis is the alternative
explanation: ANOVA assumes independent observations, roughly normal residuals and homogeneity of variance. When normality fails with small samples, Kruskal-Wallis compares the group medians using ranks (Day 17).
distractor_notes: Unequal sizes are fine, and paired tests are for two related measurements.
Equal means is H₀, not an assumption; chi-square is for counts.
Regression is for a continuous x.

stem: In a sample of 300 invoices, 45 had errors. Test whether the error proportion is 0.10. What is the Z statistic?
distractor_notes: 0.05 is the difference in proportions, not divided by its standard error.
14.4 divides by the variance instead of its square root.
2.43 uses p̂ (0.15) in the standard error instead of p₀; that is the interval formula, not the test.

stem: Of 300 web orders, 27 produced an invoice error; of 300 phone orders, 12 did. What is the 2-proportion Z statistic (web minus phone)?
distractor_notes: 5.00 is the difference in percentage points.
0.05 is the difference in proportions, not divided by its standard error.
1.24 uses only one sample's 1/n in the standard error.

stem: A team wants to know whether the proportion of late deliveries differs between two depots. Which test applies?
options: 2-sample t-test
2-proportion test
1-sample variance test
Paired t-test
explanation: Late or not is attribute data, and there are two independent groups, so the 2-proportion test (equivalently a 2 × 2 chi-square) is correct. t-tests need continuous data (Day 18).
distractor_notes: t-tests compare means of continuous data.
The variance test is for a continuous spread.
Nothing is measured twice on the same units.

stem: In a sample of 300 invoices, 45 had errors (15%). What is the margin of error of the 95% confidence interval for the proportion?
distractor_notes: 0.0206 is the standard error without multiplying by 1.96.
0.0808 doubles the margin (the full interval width).

stem:
Output from a 2-proportion test comparing the proportion of invoices with errors for web and phone orders reads:

```
Sample   X    N   Sample p
Web     27  300   0.090
Phone   12  300   0.040
Difference = p(Web) - p(Phone)
Estimate for difference:  0.05
95% CI for difference:  (0.0105, 0.0895)
Test for difference = 0 (vs not = 0):  Z = 2.48  P-Value = 0.013
```

What is the conclusion at alpha = 0.05?
options: The test is invalid because the counts are below 30
Reject; web orders have a significantly higher error proportion, by about 5 percentage points
Reject; phone orders have the higher error proportion
Fail to reject; the proportions are the same
explanation: p = 0.013 < 0.05: the proportions differ. The difference web minus phone is +0.05 and the interval excludes zero. Web orders have the higher error rate (Day 18).
distractor_notes: The counts (27, 12, 273, 288) are all well above 5, so the approximation is fine.
The positive difference favours web as the higher rate.
p < 0.05 and the interval excludes zero.

stem: A supplier claims its defect rate is 15%. In a sample of 200 parts, 24 are defective (12%). Testing H₁: p < 0.15 (one-sided), what is the p-value and the decision?
options: 0.883; reject, the rate is lower
0.012; reject
0.235; fail to reject
0.117; fail to reject, the sample does not show a lower rate
explanation: Z = (0.12 − 0.15) ÷ √(0.15 × 0.85 ÷ 200) = −0.03 ÷ 0.02525 = −1.19. One-sided p = P(Z < −1.19) = 0.117 > 0.05: fail to reject. A 12% sample rate is consistent with a 15% true rate at this sample size (Day 18).
distractor_notes: 0.883 is 1 − p, the wrong tail, and a p-value that large never rejects.
0.012 is not the p-value here.
0.235 is the two-sided p-value; the test is one-sided.

stem: A contingency table has 2 rows (clerks) and 3 columns (error types). What are the degrees of freedom for the chi-square test of independence?
explanation: df = (rows − 1) × (columns − 1) = 1 × 2 = 2 (Day 18).
distractor_notes: 6 is rows × columns.
1 would be a 2 × 2 table.
5 is rows × columns − 1.

stem: In a contingency table the Site A row totals 60, the Error column totals 65 and the grand total is 120. What is the expected count for the Site A/Error cell?
explanation: Expected count = row total × column total ÷ grand total = 60 × 65 ÷ 120 = 32.5 (Day 18).
distractor_notes: 40.0 might be the observed count; the expected count is calculated from the margins.
30.0 is half the row total, ignoring the column total.
62.5 averages the two totals.

stem: A 2 × 2 table has observed counts Site A: 40 errors, 20 no error; Site B: 25 errors, 35 no error. What is the chi-square statistic?
distractor_notes: 3.78 is half the statistic (only one row summed).
1.00 is a single cell's contribution rounded down.
15.1 doubles it.

stem: A chi-square test of independence gives p = 0.002 for error type against clerk. Which statement is correct?
options: Error type and clerk are associated: the mix of error types differs between clerks
The two clerks make the same total number of errors
The test identifies which error type each clerk makes most often
The clerk is the cause of the errors, since p is below 0.05
explanation: A significant chi-square shows association between the two categorical variables. It does not establish causation, and identifying which cells drive the result needs a look at the cell contributions (Day 18).
distractor_notes: The test is about the distribution of types, not the total count.
The test statistic alone does not say which cells differ.
Association is not causation; the clerks may differ in the orders they receive.

stem:
Software output for a chi-square test reads:

```
Pearson Chi-Square = 15.33, DF = 2, P-Value = 0.000
2 cells with expected counts less than 5
```

What should the analyst do?
options: Report the result as significant, since p is far below 0.05
Switch to a 2-sample t-test on the counts
Treat the p-value as unreliable; combine sparse categories or collect more data, then re-test
Report the result as not significant, since the expected counts are low
explanation: The chi-square approximation needs expected counts of at least 5 in each cell. Small expected counts make the p-value unreliable, however small it looks. Combine categories or gather more data (Day 18).
distractor_notes: The warning means the p-value cannot be trusted as printed.
t-tests are for continuous data.
Low expected counts make the p-value unreliable in either direction, not automatically non-significant.

stem: How does a chi-square test on a 2 × 2 contingency table relate to a 2-proportion test on the same data?
options: The 2-proportion test needs larger samples than chi-square
The chi-square test is always the more powerful of the two
They are equivalent: χ² equals Z² and the two-tailed p-values match
They test different hypotheses about the two groups
explanation: For two groups and a yes/no outcome, the 2 × 2 chi-square and the two-tailed 2-proportion test give identical p-values; χ² = Z². The proportion test adds a confidence interval for the difference (Day 18).
distractor_notes: The sample size requirements are the same.
They have the same power because they are the same test.
Both test whether the two proportions are equal.

stem: Which test is the non-parametric equivalent of the 2-sample t-test?
options: Kruskal-Wallis test
Friedman test
Mann-Whitney test
1-sample sign test
explanation: Mann-Whitney (the Wilcoxon rank-sum test) compares the medians of two independent groups by ranking all values together. Kruskal-Wallis is for three or more groups, Friedman for related groups, the sign test for one sample (Day 19).
distractor_notes: Kruskal-Wallis is the ANOVA equivalent.
Friedman is for blocked designs with three or more conditions.
The sign test compares one sample with a target.

stem:
Mann-Whitney output comparing dispute resolution times (hours) for web and phone orders reads:

```
        N   Median
Web     8   14.50
Phone   8   22.00
Point estimate for η1 - η2 is -7.50
95.9 Percent CI for η1 - η2 is (-12.00, -3.00)
Test of η1 = η2 vs η1 ≠ η2 is significant at 0.0047
```

What is the conclusion at alpha = 0.05?
options: The medians differ: phone resolution times are higher, by an estimated 7.5 hours, and the interval excludes zero
The test is invalid because the samples are small
Fail to reject, because the confidence level is not 95%
The means differ by 7.5
explanation: p = 0.0047 < 0.05. η is the symbol for a median; the estimate η₁ − η₂ = −7.5 means group 1 (web) is lower. Rank-based intervals take odd confidence levels such as 95.9%; that is normal (Day 19).
distractor_notes: Small samples are exactly when Mann-Whitney is used.
95.9% is the closest achievable level for a rank-based interval; the test still rejects.
Non-parametric tests compare medians, not means.

stem: Which test compares the medians of three or more independent groups when the data are not normal?
options: 2-proportion test
One-way ANOVA
Kruskal-Wallis test
Paired t-test
explanation: Kruskal-Wallis is the non-parametric one-way ANOVA: it ranks all values and tests whether at least one group's median differs, comparing its H statistic with chi-square on k − 1 df (Day 19).
distractor_notes: Proportion tests are for attribute data.
ANOVA assumes normal residuals.
Paired tests are for two related measurements.

stem: A Kruskal-Wallis test across four depots gives H = 11.2, df = 3, p = 0.011. What does this tell the team, and what is the next step?
options: At least one depot's median differs; pairwise follow-up shows which
All four depots differ from one another; no further analysis is needed
The four depots do not differ, since H is below the critical value
The depot medians differ by 11.2 days
explanation: Like ANOVA, a significant Kruskal-Wallis only says the groups are not all the same. Pairwise comparisons (with alpha protection) identify which depots differ (Day 19).
distractor_notes: A significant result does not mean every group differs from every other.
p = 0.011 rejects equality; H = 11.2 exceeds the critical value for 3 df (7.81).
H is a test statistic, not a difference.

stem: When would Mood's median test be chosen over the Kruskal-Wallis test?
options: When the data are normally distributed
When the data contain outliers or the groups have very different spreads
When there are only two groups to compare
When the highest possible power is needed
explanation: Mood's median test counts values above and below the overall median and runs a chi-square on the counts, which makes it insensitive to extreme values and to unequal spread. Kruskal-Wallis is more powerful when those problems are absent (Day 19).
distractor_notes: Normal data would use ANOVA.
Both tests handle two or more groups.
Mood's is less powerful, not more.

stem: How does Mood's median test compare groups?
options: By comparing the group means with the F statistic
By ranking all values together and comparing rank sums
By pairing values across groups and testing the differences
By counting values above and below the overall median and applying chi-square
explanation: Mood's reduces each value to above or below the grand median and tests the resulting contingency table with chi-square, which is why it is robust but less powerful than rank-sum methods (Day 19).
distractor_notes: F on means is ANOVA.
Ranking all values is Mann-Whitney or Kruskal-Wallis.
Pairing is for related samples.

stem: Twelve operators each assembled a part using three different fixtures, and assembly times are skewed. Which test compares the fixtures?
options: One-way ANOVA
Mann-Whitney test
Friedman test
Kruskal-Wallis test
explanation: Each operator is a block measured under every condition, so the design is blocked with three related conditions and non-normal data: Friedman. Kruskal-Wallis would ignore the blocking and treat the 36 times as independent (Day 19).
distractor_notes: ANOVA assumes normality and ignores the blocks.
Mann-Whitney is for two independent groups.
Kruskal-Wallis assumes independent groups; here the same operators appear in every group.

stem: Which parametric design does the Friedman test correspond to?
options: A one-way ANOVA with independent groups
A chi-square test of independence on counts
A 2-sample t-test with independent groups
A repeated-measures (blocked) ANOVA with three or more conditions
explanation: Friedman assigns ranks within each block (each unit measured under every condition), removing unit-to-unit differences, and tests whether the conditions differ. It extends the paired test to three or more conditions (Day 19).
distractor_notes: Independent groups would use Kruskal-Wallis.
Chi-square is for categorical counts.
Two groups would use Mann-Whitney or Wilcoxon.

stem: What does the 1-sample sign test use from the data?
options: The mean and standard deviation of the values
The variance of the differences from the target
Only whether each value is above or below the target
The ranks of the absolute differences from the target
explanation: The sign test counts values above and below the hypothesised median and tests the split against 50:50 with the binomial distribution. It uses the least information of any test, so it has the least power, but it works for any data including ordinal scores (Day 19).
distractor_notes: Means and standard deviations are for parametric tests.
Variances are for the chi-square variance test.
Ranked absolute differences are the Wilcoxon test.

stem: For which of these data would the 1-sample sign test be appropriate where the Wilcoxon test would not?
options: Normally distributed fill weights from a large sample
Satisfaction scores on a 1-to-5 scale, whose differences from the target have no numeric meaning
Pass/fail inspection results from a sample of 50
Right-skewed cycle times with a symmetric spread of differences
explanation: The sign test needs only to know whether each value is above or below the target, so it works for ordinal data where differences have no numeric meaning. Wilcoxon ranks the sizes of differences and assumes symmetry (Day 19).
distractor_notes: Normal data would use a t-test.
Pass/fail data use a proportion test.
Symmetric differences are what Wilcoxon handles well.

stem: What does the 1-sample Wilcoxon test use from the data that the sign test does not?
options: The ranked sizes of the differences from the target, as well as their signs
The variance of the values
The mean of the values
The number of values equal to the target
explanation: Wilcoxon ranks the absolute differences from the hypothesised median and sums the ranks of the positive and negative differences. Using the sizes gives it more power than the sign test, at the cost of assuming a symmetric distribution (Day 19).
distractor_notes: Variance is not used.
The mean is a parametric quantity.
Values equal to the target are dropped by both tests.

stem: Which assumption does the 1-sample Wilcoxon test make that the sign test does not?
options: The data are attribute data
The distribution is symmetric about the median
The sample size is at least 30
The data are normally distributed
explanation: Wilcoxon assumes symmetry so that the ranked positive and negative differences are comparable. It does not assume normality. The sign test assumes nothing about shape (Day 19).
distractor_notes: Both tests are for continuous or ordinal data, not attribute data.
Wilcoxon works with small samples.
Normality is the parametric assumption; Wilcoxon does not need it.

stem: Resolution times for 8 disputed web-order invoices and 8 phone-order invoices are heavily skewed. The team wants to know whether the two order types differ. Which test should be used, and why?
options: Paired t-test, since the two groups are the same size
Mann-Whitney test, since the data are non-normal and the samples are small
2-sample t-test, since there are two independent groups
Chi-square test, since the data are skewed
explanation: Two independent groups, continuous Y, non-normal and only 8 per group: the t-test's p-value is unreliable, so the rank-based Mann-Whitney test is the right choice (Day 19).
distractor_notes: Equal sizes do not make the groups paired; the invoices are different units.
Two groups alone does not justify a t-test when the data are skewed and small.
Chi-square is for categorical counts.

stem: Repair times from three workshops are compared. Each workshop supplied 10 skewed values with no extreme outliers. Which test is most appropriate?
options: Kruskal-Wallis test
Friedman test
One-way ANOVA
Mood's median test
explanation: Three independent groups, non-normal continuous data, no outliers: Kruskal-Wallis has more power than Mood's median and does not assume normality like ANOVA. Friedman needs a blocked design (Day 19).
distractor_notes: The workshops are independent groups, not blocks.
ANOVA assumes normal residuals; 10 skewed values per group is too few to rely on the central limit theorem.
Mood's would be preferred only if outliers or very unequal spreads were present.

stem: Four call centres are compared on handling time. The data are skewed and one centre has several extreme values from system outages. Which test is the safer choice?
options: Friedman test
Mood's median test
One-way ANOVA
Kruskal-Wallis test
explanation: With extreme values present, Mood's median test is the robust choice: it only asks whether each value is above or below the grand median, so outages cannot dominate. Kruskal-Wallis is more powerful but more affected by unequal spread (Day 19).
distractor_notes: Friedman needs a blocked design; the centres are independent groups.
ANOVA is the least robust to outliers.
Kruskal-Wallis is more sensitive to outliers and unequal spreads than Mood's.

stem: Eight nurses each recorded the time to complete a task using four different checklists. Times are not normal. Which test compares the checklists?
options: 1-sample Wilcoxon test
Mann-Whitney test for each pair of checklists
Kruskal-Wallis test on the 32 times
Friedman test with nurse as the block
explanation: Each nurse tried every checklist, so nurse is a block and the four conditions are related. Friedman ranks within each nurse and tests whether the checklists differ (Day 19).
distractor_notes: Wilcoxon tests one sample against a target.
Six pairwise Mann-Whitney tests inflate the Type I risk and ignore blocking.
Kruskal-Wallis would treat the 32 times as independent and ignore the nurse effect.

stem: A standard says disputes should be resolved within a median of 12 hours. Of 10 recorded times, one equals 12, 7 are above and 2 below. A two-sided sign test gives p = 0.18. What is the conclusion?
options: Reject H₀: the median is above 12 hours
Fail to reject H₀: the sign test cannot detect one-sided differences
Reject H₀: the tied value must be counted as above the target
Fail to reject H₀: 7 above and 2 below is not far enough from an even split
explanation: The sign test drops the value equal to the target and tests 7 of 9 against a 50:50 split; with so few values that is not significant (p = 0.18). More data, or the more powerful Wilcoxon test, is needed before the standard is challenged (Day 19).
distractor_notes: The sign test can be run one-sided; the problem here is the small sample.
Ties with the target are dropped, not counted.

stem: Ten paired differences are 3.1, −0.4, 2.2, 1.8, 0.6, 2.9, 1.1, −0.2, 2.4, 1.5. The 1-sample Wilcoxon test of H₀: median difference = 0 (two-sided) gives what p-value?
explanation: Ranking the absolute differences and summing the ranks of the two negative values (−0.2 and −0.4 are the two smallest, ranks 1 and 2) gives a very small negative rank sum; the two-sided p-value is 0.0098, so H₀ is rejected. The sign test on the same data (8 of 10 positive) would give p = 0.11 (Day 19).
distractor_notes: 0.3594 doubles the sign-test value.
0.05 is alpha, not the p-value.
0.1797 is the sign-test p-value for a 7-of-9 split, not the Wilcoxon result.

stem: In a multi-vari study, a difference in average thickness between the morning and afternoon shifts is which family of variation?
options: Cyclical
Temporal
Positional
Within-piece
explanation: Shift to shift is a change over time: temporal (time-to-time) variation. Positional is within one unit; cyclical is between consecutive units (Day 20).
distractor_notes: Cyclical variation is between consecutive units made under the same conditions.
Positional variation is across positions within one unit.
Within-piece is another name for positional.

stem: A four-cavity mould produces brackets; cavity 3 is consistently wider than the other three. Which family of variation is this?
options: Cyclical
Lot-to-lot
Temporal
Positional
explanation: Cavity is a position within one shot, so the difference is positional variation, pointing to a spatial cause such as tooling (Day 20).
distractor_notes: Cyclical would be differences between consecutive shots.
No lots are described.
Nothing here changes over time.

stem: What kind of study is a multi-vari analysis?
options: A formal hypothesis test comparing two or more means
An active experiment in which factors are deliberately changed
A passive graphical study of the running process by position, unit and time
A control chart with specification limits added
explanation: Multi-vari samples the process as it runs without changing anything, and plots the results by position, unit and time so the largest family of variation is visible. It narrows the search before hypothesis tests (Day 20).
distractor_notes: It is graphical, not a formal test.
Deliberate changes belong to designed experiments, which are beyond this course.
It is not a control chart.

stem: On a multi-vari chart the vertical lines within each unit are short, the unit averages within each time period are close together, but the cluster averages move steadily upward across the shift. Which family dominates and what kind of cause is likely?
options: Temporal; look for warm-up, tool wear or ambient conditions
Cyclical; look for a material lot or technique cause
Positional; look for a tooling or fixture cause
None; the process shows only common cause variation
explanation: Short within-unit lines mean little positional variation, tight unit clusters mean little cyclical variation, and the drift of the clusters across time is temporal variation. Look for something that changes over the shift (Day 20).
distractor_notes: Cyclical variation would show as spread among the units in a cluster.
Positional variation would show as long vertical lines.
A steady drift is a real, identifiable pattern.

stem: In multi-vari terminology, what is cyclical (piece-to-piece) variation?
options: Variation between shifts or days
Variation between consecutive units made under the same conditions
Variation caused by the measurement system
Variation between positions on the same unit
explanation: Cyclical variation is unit-to-unit: shot 1 to shot 2 to shot 3 at the same time point. It points to causes acting on each unit, such as material or technique (Day 20).
distractor_notes: That is temporal.
Measurement variation is studied with MSA, not multi-vari.
That is positional.

stem: The number of scratches found on each painted panel follows which distribution?
options: Poisson
Binomial
Exponential
Normal
explanation: A count of events per unit, where events occur independently at an average rate, is Poisson. Binomial would be the number of defective panels in a fixed sample; exponential the time between events (Day 20).
distractor_notes: Binomial counts successes out of a fixed number of trials, such as defective panels in a sample of 50.
Exponential models time between events.
Counts are discrete, not normal.

stem: The number of defective parts in a random sample of 50 from a line with a 4% defect rate follows which distribution?
options: Normal
Weibull
Binomial
Poisson
explanation: A fixed number of trials (50), each defective or not with the same probability (0.04): binomial with n = 50 and p = 0.04, mean 2. Poisson would model defects per part rather than defective parts out of n (Day 20).
distractor_notes: The count is discrete and small; not normal.
Weibull models time to failure.
Poisson models counts of events per unit or interval, not successes out of a fixed n.

stem: Deliveries are late with probability 0.10. In a sample of 20 deliveries, what is the expected (mean) number of late deliveries?
explanation: For a binomial distribution the mean is n × p = 20 × 0.10 = 2.0 late deliveries. The standard deviation is √(20 × 0.1 × 0.9) = 1.34 (Day 20).
distractor_notes: 0.5 is p × 5, an arbitrary figure; the mean uses the full n of 20.
1.34 is the standard deviation, not the mean.

stem: A Weibull fit to bearing failure times gives a shape parameter of 2.4. What does this indicate?
options: That the data are Poisson
A failure rate that increases with age: wear-out
Early-life (infant mortality) failures
A constant failure rate
explanation: Weibull shape β above 1 means the failure rate rises with age, the wear-out pattern, so preventive replacement makes sense. β = 1 is the constant-rate exponential; β below 1 is early-life failure (Day 20).
distractor_notes: Weibull is a continuous life distribution, unrelated to Poisson counts.
Early-life failures are β < 1.
A constant rate is β = 1.

stem: Panels average 2.0 scratches each, following a Poisson distribution. What is the probability that a panel has no scratches?
distractor_notes: 0.8647 is 1 − P(0), the probability of at least one scratch.
0.2707 is the probability of exactly one scratch.
0.5 has no basis in the Poisson formula.

stem: A pump fails at a constant rate of 0.02 failures per hour. What is its mean time between failures?
options: 0.02 hours
20 hours
50 hours
34.7 hours
explanation: For an exponential distribution with rate λ the mean is 1 ÷ λ = 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 hours. The median is lower, 50 × ln 2 = 34.7 hours (Day 20).
distractor_notes: 0.02 is the rate, not the mean time.
20 hours would be 1 ÷ 0.05.
34.7 hours is the median, not the mean.

stem: Which statement about the exponential distribution is correct?
options: It is symmetric, with its mean equal to its median
It models the number of events in a fixed interval, with variance equal to mean
It is a discrete distribution with whole-number outcomes
It models the time between random events at a constant rate, with median below mean
explanation: The exponential is continuous and right-skewed, starting high at zero and decaying, with mean 1 ÷ λ and median 0.693 ÷ λ. Counts of events in an interval are Poisson (Day 20).
distractor_notes: The exponential is strongly right-skewed.
Counts in an interval are Poisson; the exponential is the time between them.
Time is continuous.

stem: Deliveries are late with probability 0.10, independently. What is the probability that none of 20 deliveries is late?
explanation: P(0) = (1 − p)^n = 0.90²⁰ = 0.1216. Note this is a binomial calculation; the Poisson approximation with λ = 2 gives 0.1353, close but not the same (Day 20).
distractor_notes: The probability is small but not zero.
0.1353 is the Poisson approximation e^(−2), not the exact binomial value.
0.90 is the probability that one delivery is on time.

stem: Count data from a process have a mean of 3.1 defects per unit and a variance of 3.0. What does this suggest?
options: The counts are not Poisson, since the variance is not exactly the mean
The counts are binomial, since the variance is below the mean
The counts are approximately Poisson, since the variance is close to the mean
The counts are normal, since the mean is above 3
explanation: For a Poisson distribution the variance equals the mean. A variance close to the mean is consistent with Poisson; a variance much larger than the mean would indicate clustering of events (Day 20).
distractor_notes: Slight differences are sampling variation; equality is the Poisson property.
Binomial variance n·p·(1 − p) is smaller than the mean, but a fixed n is not described and the gap here is negligible.
Counts of defects are discrete and small.
